content: To address public health needs effectively, additional clinical research sites should be established within relevant communities. These Clinical Trial Units (CTUs) can then access disease-specific expertise as required. The World Health Organization (WHO) is developing a CTU maturity framework, which will be particularly beneficial for countries without pre-existing systems by providing a standardized structure for developing such units. This framework will include a tiered system with metrics tailored to the CTU’s purpose and level of functional maturity. For example, the infrastructure required for CTUs serving as regional or national hubs for large trials will differ from that needed for smaller, local CTUs that feed into these hubs. Strengthening access to healthcare and clinical facilities is essential to facilitate clinical research and integrate it into routine national healthcare systems across all care settings, including home, community, primary, secondary, and tertiary care. Embedding clinical trials into point-of-care processes offers significant benefits, such as cost and efficiency savings, increased staff involvement in research, and broader awareness and enthusiasm for clinical trials. Expanding trial sites from large national centers to smaller local centers or even patients’ homes, as seen in decentralized trials, can enhance sample size, statistical power, and representativeness, leading to more meaningful results that improve patient care. The adoption of automated and digital processes should be encouraged globally to increase the speed, efficiency, and transparency of clinical trials. Building affordable, sustainable, and efficient electronic healthcare systems will enable long-term research connectivity. However, these systems must be designed to be accessible and practical. Best practices for clinical trials should include supporting the careers of clinical researchers through local programs and funding options at all career stages, including leadership roles in clinical research. The UNICEF/UNDP/World Bank/WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases has outlined a Global Competency Framework for Clinical Research, which identifies the competencies required for a clinical research team to conduct a successful study. This framework can be applied to any research study, regardless of size, location, disease focus, or type of research. Efforts should also focus on addressing barriers to recruiting and training individuals interested in clinical research. Requirements such as prior clinical trial experience or specific academic qualifications may exclude promising candidates, particularly those with limited financial resources or from underrepresented demographics. A well-functioning clinical trial ecosystem requires patient and community engagement, collaboration, use of standardized systems, training, risk-proportionate approaches, sustainability, innovation, and transparency. This engagement should be a continuous process, not limited to pre-trial campaigns. Expertise in community engagement should be developed as a core skill for designing and conducting clinical trials. Feedback mechanisms must be in place to demonstrate how patient input and data are utilized, as a lack of transparency can undermine trust and future participation. High-quality clinical trials require effective communication and collaboration among all stakeholders to share ideas, reduce duplication, build capacity, and maximize resources. Clinical research networks and disease-specific consortia play a crucial role in enabling coordination, accelerating evidence generation, and reducing waste. Examples include the European Clinical Research Infrastructure Network (ECRIN), the UK’s National Institute for Health and Care Research Clinical Research Network (NIHR CRN), and the pan-Canadian Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) consortium. However, gaps in such networks exist in regions like Latin America, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, and parts of Asia, highlighting the need for further collaboration and initiatives. Training and mentoring are critical for building clinical trial capacity. Accessible and fit-for-purpose training packages should be developed to enhance understanding of trial design, implementation, and reporting principles, as well as ethical considerations. Training should target all levels of the clinical trial infrastructure, including community-based settings, patient advocacy groups, research coordinators, ethics committee members, and regulatory agencies. Robust training in statistical methodology and clinical data management is essential to enable appropriate sample size estimations and support the design of larger, well-conducted trials. Innovation in trial design, such as adaptive platform and cluster designs, should be promoted to improve efficiency and expand the scope of potential outcomes. Digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, wearable biosensors, and connected devices, offer opportunities to enhance trial efficiency and inclusivity. These advancements require an agile approach from researchers and regulators to balance innovation with risk mitigation. Transparency is imperative across all aspects of clinical trials to foster trust, improve efficiency, and facilitate data sharing. This includes the timely reporting of both positive and negative results, registration in publicly accessible trial registries, and open-access publication of findings. During public health emergencies, rapid activation of pre-approved protocols and coordination among stakeholders are essential to meet urgent health needs. Standing network arrangements and standardized protocols can accelerate timelines, while funders should encourage data sharing and the use of master protocols to aggregate data across trials. In conclusion, clinical trials have the potential to transform healthcare and improve quality of life globally. To achieve this, they must be reliable, ethical, and efficient, addressing scientifically important questions relevant to the populations they aim to benefit. This requires partnerships with patients and communities, equitable funding, and global collaboration.
